regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 55.9","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY and PMI Composite at 55.9 look unambiguous — until you note that core sector growth slipped to 4.8% YoY from 5.0%, and IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY sits at only the 52nd percentile despite the headline euphoria. The quality of growth is bifurcated: services credit surging at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile) is doing the heavy lifting while goods-economy proxies are more modest. Invert the bull case: if this is a services-led expansion with manufacturing PMI at 55.1 but core sector decelerating, the multiplier effect on employment and rural income is weaker than the headline implies.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 5.54% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY has risen from 3.21% in two months — but the decomposition matters more than the level. Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile, highest in the dataset) is the structural driver; food at 7.74% YoY is accelerating; core CPI at 3.9% YoY sits at only the 28th percentile. The gap between a benign core and a punishing headline tells you this is a supply-side squeeze, not demand overheating — which makes RBI's job harder, not easier. Cutting into a 22.93% fuel print would be a policy error; holding with core at 3.9% is defensible but increasingly uncomfortable for growth advocates.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.4% YoY; CD ratio 81%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.4% YoY against deposits at 17.8% YoY — a 160 bps divergence — keeps the CD ratio at 81% (73rd percentile historically). The more telling signal is the sectoral composition: services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile, rising two consecutive months) and vehicle credit jumping from 8.7% to 19.7% YoY suggest the acceleration is broad, not concentrated. The last time India sustained a CD ratio above 80% while the repo rate was on hold, the subsequent macro-prudential response came via risk-weight tightening on unsecured lending — the RBI's preferred instrument when it cannot use the rate lever. Watch for that circular before the next MPC.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. (38th percentile) looks accommodative in isolation; against CPI at 5.54% YoY, the real rate is barely positive at roughly -30 bps. The RBI's own inflation forecast has risen to 5.1% YoY — 40 bps above its prior estimate — which arithmetically closes the door on any near-term cut. For housing, an average home loan rate of 8.4% p.a. against an affordability index at a 10-year-worst 10.9× price-to-income means the rate pause is not benign for residential demand. For FX, a near-zero real rate with INR at 95.24 and FII outflows at ₹49,935 cr / month is a fragile equilibrium.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile, up from 75.6%) confirm the investment upcycle is real. The inversion: private capex typically accelerates when utilisation crosses 80% — at 77.4%, there is still 250 bps of headroom before the private sector feels compelled to invest rather than sweat existing assets. The bull case requires utilisation to keep climbing; the bear case is that credit tightening (via macro-prudential measures) raises the cost of capex financing before utilisation reaches that threshold.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹203521 cr/mo; PV 7.9% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,03,521 cr / month (73rd percentile) is solid but not accelerating — the prior month was ₹1,99,853 cr / month, a modest uptick. Passenger vehicle sales at 7.9% YoY are decelerating (down from 16% and 26.1% in prior months), while two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY signal rural/mass-market recovery. The divergence is the story: premium urban consumption (retail mall vacancy at a 10-year-low 4.8% vacant) is robust, while mass-market vehicle demand is only now recovering. Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY is a regressive tax on the informal economy — the segment that two-wheeler sales measure — and the recovery there is more fragile than the GST headline suggests.","badge_label":"Stable Consumption","badge_type":"b-neu"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.4% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160 bps divergence widening for 2 consecutive months (17.1%→19.4% credit; 9.9%→17.8% deposits). CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits, down from 82.2% but still at 73rd percentile historically. NBFC credit accelerating at 15.8% YoY (up from 10% YoY), now at 57th percentile. Services credit surging at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile), rising 2 straight months.","implication":"The deposit acceleration masks structural stress: banks are chasing credit growth via wholesale funding and NBFC partnerships. Overweight private banks with CASA ratios >45% and deposit-to-liability ratios >70% — they can poach retail deposits. Underweight NBFCs with wholesale funding >30% of liabilities; their funding costs will spike if RBI tightens liquidity. Watch for RBI to signal CRR cuts or OMO purchases within 6 weeks to ease deposit pressure.","pct_10y":73,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 73rd percentile is elevated but not crisis-level; historically, ratios >85% preceded NBFC stress (2018-19). Current divergence suggests late-cycle credit demand outpacing retail deposit mobilisation.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Upcycle Broadens Beyond Goods","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (52nd percentile), up from 16.1% YoY. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile), up from 75.6%. Services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile) — the highest in the dataset — rising 2 consecutive months (22.9%→24.3%). Agricultural credit at 17.2% YoY (78th percentile), rising 3 straight months. Vehicle credit at 19.7% YoY (68th percentile), up from 8.7% YoY.","implication":"Capex is no longer confined to manufacturing; services (IT, telecom, logistics) and agri-tech are driving credit demand. Overweight capital goods manufacturers, logistics, and agri-tech plays. Increase exposure to companies with order books >12 months and ROIC >15%. Avoid low-utilisation capacity plays; the 77.4% CU level leaves room for organic growth without new capex, but rising credit suggests confidence in demand sustainability.","pct_10y":74,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is mid-cycle; historically, sustained >78% CU preceded 18-24 month capex booms (2014-15, 2021-22). Services credit at 79th percentile is a new signal — suggests GCC expansion and IT infrastructure buildout.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Inflows Hit 93rd Percentile, Ticket Size Rising","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile), rising 3 consecutive months (₹29,845→₹31,961→₹32,297→₹32,490 cr / month). SIP accounts at 10.06 mn (2nd percentile, data quality issue noted). SIP AUM at ₹17.86 lakh cr (89th percentile), up from ₹16.64 lakh cr. Equity MF net inflows at ₹38,307 cr / month (80th percentile), up from ₹29,329 cr / month. DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile). NFO collections collapsed to ₹998 cr / month (2nd percentile) from ₹3,051 cr / month.","implication":"SIP inflows are genuine, but NFO collapse signals retail is NOT chasing new schemes — they're dollar-cost-averaging into existing equity funds. This is late-cycle behaviour: affluent retail entering via systematic plans, not lump-sum allocations. Overweight large-cap, dividend-paying stocks; underweight small-cap and growth. The ₹32,490 cr / month SIP run-rate, if sustained, will add ₹390k cr AUM annually — a 4.7% organic boost to MF industry AUM.","pct_10y":93,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 93rd percentile preceded market corrections in 2022 and 2018; however, the absence of NFO demand (2nd percentile) suggests retail is risk-averse and locking into systematic plans rather than chasing performance.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation at 95th Percentile, CAD Risk Rising","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile), up from 20.05% YoY — the highest in the dataset. Brent crude at $111.66 / bbl (77th percentile), up from $109.9 / bbl over 3 months. WTI at $103.44 / bbl (84th percentile). FAO food index at 136 index (61st percentile), up from 128.5 index. Food inflation at 7.74% YoY (57th percentile), rising 2 consecutive months (5.52%→7.74%). Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY (52nd percentile), up from 3.21% YoY.","implication":"Fuel and food inflation are the twin drivers of headline CPI overshoot. RBI's 5.1% inflation forecast (53rd percentile) is at risk; actual CPI will likely stay >5.5% through Q2 FY27. This constrains RBI rate cuts to H2 FY27 at earliest. India's oil import bill is rising; with INR at 95.24 ₹ / USD (89th percentile, weakening), CAD will widen. Hedge INR exposure; reduce long-duration bond positions; overweight energy stocks with pricing power (refiners, integrated oil majors).","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile last occurred in 2022 (post-Russia invasion) and 2008 (pre-GFC). Current level suggests geopolitical oil risk or supply-side shock; CAD widening risk is material.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"BOJ Tightening Breaks Carry Trade Consensus","data_text":"BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile), up from 0.75% p.a. — the highest in the dataset, rising 2 consecutive months (1%→1.25%). Fed funds rate at 3.75% p.a. (68th percentile mid), up from 3.63% p.a., rising 2 in a row. ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (63rd percentile), up from 2% p.a., rising 2 in a row. US 10Y Treasury yield at 4.96% (90th percentile), down from 5.13% but still elevated. US PMI composite at 58.4 index (91st percentile), rising 2 consecutive months (56→58.4). Global PMI composite at 54.3 index (84th percentile).","implication":"BOJ's 125 bps rate hike cycle is unwinding the yen carry trade that funded global risk assets. With Fed on pause and ECB tightening, the liquidity backdrop is shifting from 'easy' to 'selective'. US equity valuations (S&P 500 at 100th percentile, Nasdaq at 70th percentile) are vulnerable to carry unwind. Reduce leverage; trim long-duration growth positions; overweight defensive sectors and dividend payers. Monitor yen strength (JPY weakness vs USD) as a leading indicator of carry trade stress.","pct_10y":100,"pct_note":"BOJ at 100th percentile is a regime shift; last time BOJ was this hawkish was 2019 (pre-COVID). Carry trade unwind typically precedes 3-6 month equity volatility spikes.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Weakening as FII Flows Turn Negative","data_text":"INR at 95.24 ₹ / USD (89th percentile, weakening), up from 94.93 ₹ / USD. FII equity net at -₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile, outflow), a sharp reversal from +₹29,631 cr / month 2 months prior. India VIX at 16.86 index (12th percentile, elevated), up from 15.76 index. DXY at 101.752 index (54th percentile), flat. US 10Y Treasury at 4.96% yield (90th percentile), down from 5.13% but still a carry headwind.","implication":"FII outflows are accelerating as US yields remain elevated and BOJ tightening raises carry costs. FII outflows at 17th percentile suggest foreign investors are rotating out of India; this is a regime shift from 2023-24 inflows.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Collapse Signals GCC Saturation","data_text":"Office absorption at 5.3 mn sq ft / quarter (0th percentile, lowest in dataset), down from 13.2 mn sq ft / quarter 5 quarters ago. Office vacancy at 11.4% vacant (25th percentile), up from 10.6% vacant. Nifty IT index flat YTD despite 7.8% GDP growth and 55.9 PMI composite (85th percentile). Bank Nifty at 54,287 (89th percentile, strong), but IT stocks lagging. Services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile) — the highest in dataset — yet office absorption is collapsing. Rent in Bengaluru at ₹109 / sqft / month (61st percentile), up from ₹100.6 / sqft / month, but absorption falling.","implication":"Global Capability Centers (GCCs) are the office buyer, not traditional IT services. GCCs are consolidating into fewer, larger campuses (hence rising rents in prime locations but falling total absorption). This decouples IT services from commercial real estate — a structural shift. Traditional IT services companies (TCS, Infosys, Wipro) are shedding office space; GCCs (Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple) are concentrating in Bangalore and Hyderabad. Overweight GCC-beneficiary plays (real estate in Bangalore/Hyderabad, logistics, data centres). Underweight traditional IT services on valuation; they're not the office growth story anymore. Watch for office vacancy to breach 12% — that triggers landlord distress and potential REIT downgrades.","pct_10y":0,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 0th percentile is unprecedented in this dataset; it signals a structural break in India's commercial real estate model. The divergence between services credit growth (79th percentile) and office absorption (0th percentile) proves the credit is flowing to GCCs and tech infrastructure, not traditional IT services real estate.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

Services Carry the Growth Load — Goods Economy Quietly Decelerates

The facts:

  • GDP at 7.8% YoY and PMI Composite at 55.9 (85th percentile) headline a strong expansion.
  • But core sector growth slipped to 4.8% YoY from 5.0% YoY — the goods economy is not confirming the services signal.
  • Services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile, rising two consecutive months) is the real engine; manufacturing credit at 18.2% YoY is decelerating from 20.0% YoY.
  • Passenger vehicle sales fell to 7.9% YoY from 16.0% YoY — a high-frequency consumption proxy pointing to urban demand fatigue at the margin.
  • But two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY suggest rural demand is recovering, creating a split-economy signal the headline GDP cannot resolve.

The tension: GDP at 7.8% YoY is a services-and-credit story; the goods economy — core sector, PV sales, commercial vehicle sales at 12.6% YoY and falling — is telling a softer tale. The multiplier effect on employment is weaker when services lead.

Bottom line: Watch core sector YoY: a third consecutive month below 5.0% YoY would signal the goods-economy deceleration is structural, not seasonal.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

Synchronised Tightening Meets Peak Equity — Something Gives

The facts:

  • US PMI Composite at 58.4 (91st percentile, rising two consecutive months) and Global PMI at 54.3 (84th percentile) signal DM re-acceleration.
  • But US GDP SAAR at 2.2% SAAR is decelerating from 2.5% SAAR — survey optimism and hard data are diverging.
  • BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, highest in the dataset) — rising two consecutive months — is unwinding the yen carry trade that funded EM equity inflows.
  • US 10Y Treasury at 4.96% yield (90th percentile) with Fed Funds at 3.75% p.a. means bond markets are tightening independently of the Fed.
  • Nikkei at 62,693 (100th percentile) is falling despite the growth signal — the BOJ repricing is overriding the PMI tailwind.

The tension: DM PMIs are pricing re-acceleration; DM bond markets and the BOJ are pricing tighter-for-longer. One of them is wrong, and the resolution will determine whether EM carry trades — and India's FII flows — stabilise or deteriorate further.

Bottom line: BOJ's next rate decision is the single most important global event for India's FII flow trajectory; a third consecutive hike would accelerate carry unwind.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

Domestic Flows Hold — But the Architecture Is Narrowing

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile, rising three consecutive months) provide a structural floor to domestic equity demand.
  • DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile) is absorbing FII outflows of ₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile) almost exactly.
  • But NFO collections at ₹998 cr / month (2nd percentile) signal that fund houses have stopped launching — incremental retail appetite is not being mobilised.
  • MF AUM fell to ₹82.64 lakh cr from ₹87.08 lakh cr — market depreciation is eroding the AUM base that SIP flows are building.
  • Corp bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr / month (0th percentile) is at a 10-year low, suggesting the credit market is not an alternative funding channel for the real economy.

The tension: SIP autopilot is holding the equity market together, but the DII-FII offset is arithmetically precise — any acceleration in FII outflows breaks the equilibrium. The NFO collapse and AUM erosion suggest the retail bid is wide but not deepening.

Bottom line: If FII outflows exceed ₹60,000 cr / month, DII absorption capacity will be tested and Nifty support at 22,000 becomes the line to watch.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

Mall Floors Full, Flat Floors Unaffordable — A Consumer Paradox

The facts:

  • NRI buying is RISING — NRI share of residential purchases at 18% (up 8 pp vs prior period), with 25% share within premium/luxury; Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Delhi-NCR are the primary destinations.
  • Retail mall vacancy at a 10-year-low 4.8% vacant (7th percentile) confirms physical retail demand is structurally intact — the consumer is present.
  • But the affordability index at 10.9× price ÷ income (100th percentile, worst in the dataset) means the same consumer cannot buy the residential unit above the mall.
  • Hyderabad leads residential momentum — sales +15% YoY, launches +120% YoY — but 28 months of unsold inventory is a supply overhang that price appreciation of 6% YoY cannot justify.
  • Office REIT units — Embassy at ₹370, Mindspace at ₹345, Brookfield at ₹263 — are all down sharply from prior levels despite office absorption recovering to 5.3 mn sq ft / quarter.

The tension: Retail real estate is at peak occupancy while residential affordability is at a 10-year worst — the consumer has spending power for discretionary retail but not for home ownership. NRI demand is papering over the domestic affordability gap in the premium segment.

Bottom line: Overweight retail mall operators and under-allocated REITs; avoid residential developers exposed to the ₹80 lakh–₹1.5 cr premium band where affordability stress is sharpest.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Four Fuses, One Detonator — Sequencing Is Everything

The facts:

  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) with Brent at $111.66/bbl — every $10 adds ~$15 bn to India's import bill and widens CAD by ~40 bps; INR at 95.24 has limited buffer.
  • FII equity outflows at ₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile) — a reversal from +₹29,631 cr / month two months prior — with BOJ tightening the structural driver, not a one-month aberration.
  • CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits (73rd percentile) with credit growing at 19.4% YoY — macro-prudential tightening via risk weights is the RBI's most likely next move, not a rate cut.
  • Affordability index at 10.9× price ÷ income (100th percentile) with home loan rates at 8.4% p.a. — residential demand outside NRI and ultra-luxury is structurally impaired.
  • Office absorption at 5.3 mn sq ft / quarter (0th percentile) with GCC occupancy at 42% of leasing — any GCC hiring freeze in the US transmits directly to India's Grade-A office market within two quarters.

The tension: The fuel-CAD-INR chain and the BOJ carry-unwind are external risks that compound each other; the CD ratio and affordability risks are domestic and self-reinforcing. A simultaneous trigger — Brent above $120/bbl coinciding with a BOJ hike — would stress all four simultaneously.

Bottom line: Watch Brent crude this week: a sustained print above $115/bbl forces the CAD-INR-inflation feedback loop into an active phase and closes the RBI's already narrow policy space.

"}
